discoveryHook.scenario: A jacket originally priced at \$80 is put on sale for \$60. The markdown is \$20. A [[kw:markdown]] is a reduction from the original selling price, often used to clear inventory, respond to competition, or sell perishable items before they spoil.

visuals.caption: Markdown lowers the original price; markup raises the cost to get the price.
visuals.title: Markdown vs. Markup

explanation: [[kw:Markdown]] is the difference between the original selling price and the reduced sale price.
Markdown amount = Original Selling Price – Sale Price.
Sale Price = Original Selling Price – Markdown.
Markdowns are common in retail for clearance, seasonal sales, and short‑dated products.
[[imp:Markdown is not the same as markup—it reduces price, while markup increases it.]]

notes: Original price is the initial selling price before reduction.
Markdown is expressed in dollars; markdown percent is usually based on the original price.
formulaCard.title: Markdown Amount and Sale Price

teacherCues: Ask: 'What happens to prices when a store has a clearance sale?'
Write the markdown formula on the board: Sale Price = Original Price – Markdown.

confusionCorner.body: Don’t confuse markdown with markup. [[imp:Markdown reduces a selling price; markup increases cost to get a selling price.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

examples.title: A – Find percent markdown

examples.peerPrompt: Think: 'If 30% is taken off, what percent remains?'
examples.title: B – Complement strategy
examples.prompt: Explain why you can find sale price by multiplying original price by (1 – percent markdown).
steps: 100% – markdown percent = the percent of the original price you still pay.
Multiplying by this decimal gives the sale price directly.
Example: 30% off → you pay 70%, so sale = original × 0.70.

examples.title: C – Find sale price using percent
examples.prompt: A pair of shoes is originally \$80. It is marked down 35%. Find the sale price.

notes: Always convert the percent to a decimal before using in calculations.
formulaCard.title: Percent Markdown Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Percent Markdown} = \frac{\text{Markdown}}{\text{Original Price}} \times 100$$ $$\text{Markdown} = \text{Original Price} \times \text{Percent Markdown}$$ $$\text{Sale Price} = \text{Original Price} \times (1 - \text{Percent Markdown})$$

explanation: [[kw:Percent markdown]] = (Markdown Amount ÷ Original Selling Price) × 100.
The original selling price is the base (100%).
This is just like percent markup on selling price—original price is the whole.
To find the markdown amount when the percent is known: Markdown = Original Price × (Percent Markdown as decimal).
To find the sale price directly: Sale Price = Original Price × (1 – Percent Markdown).

confusionCorner.body: Don’t subtract the percent directly from the dollar amount. [[imp:Convert percent to decimal, then multiply; or subtract the markdown amount.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

challengeCorner.prompt: After a 30% markdown, a camera sells for \$210. What was the original price? Hint: Original = Sale ÷ (1 – 0.30).

Derive adjusted cost per unit = Total Cost ÷ Expected Good Units.
blocks.title: 3. Pricing Perishables to Cover Spoilage

examples.prompt: A florist buys 100 roses for \$200. She expects 15% spoilage. Find the adjusted cost per good rose.
examples.title: A – Calculate adjusted cost

examples.peerPrompt: Think about what happens to the loaves that are sold before spoilage occurs.
examples.title: B – Why not just raise price on all?
steps: If they charge \$2.78 and no loaves spoil that day, they overcharge customers.
But on average, spoilage happens, so the price needs to cover that loss.
Competition may also limit how high they can price.
examples.prompt: Explain why the bakery can't simply charge \$2.78 per loaf from the start without calculating spoilage.

steps: So each good unit costs \$3.125 to account for spoilage.
examples.prompt: Total cost \$1,000 for 400 units, spoilage rate 20%. Find adjusted cost per good unit.
examples.title: C – Find adjusted cost

discoveryHook.scenario: A bakery makes 200 loaves of bread daily at a total cost of \$500. On average, 20 loaves (10%) go stale and must be thrown away. The 180 good loaves must absorb the cost of the spoiled ones. So each loaf costs effectively \$500 ÷ 180 ≈ \$2.78, not \$2.50.

visuals.caption: Cost per unit rises because the loss is spread over fewer good units.
visuals.title: Spoilage Impact on Pricing

explanation: [[kw:Spoilage]] is the loss of unsellable items (bread, flowers, produce).
The retailer must price the remaining good units to recover the total cost of all units.
[[imp:Adjusted Cost per Unit = Total Cost ÷ Expected Good Units.]]
Expected good units = Total Units × (1 – Spoilage Rate).
Once adjusted cost is found, the retailer applies a markup (usually percent on cost) to get a selling price that covers spoilage and profit.

formulaCard.title: Adjusted Cost per Unit for Spoilage
notes: Expected Good Units = Total Units × (1 – Spoilage Rate).
Spoilage rate is expressed as a decimal.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Adjusted Cost per Unit} = \frac{\text{Total Cost}}{\text{Expected Good Units}}$$

hints: The number of units that will actually sell.
questions.prompt: Adjusted Cost per Unit = Total Cost ÷ ___.

blocks.title: 4. Markdowns on Perishable Items
teacherCues: Combine the markdown and perishable concepts.
Show that a second markdown can be applied to clear remaining stock before total spoilage.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: A markdown that reduces the sale price below adjusted cost results in a [[imp:loss per unit]]. However, selling at a loss is sometimes better than letting goods spoil completely.

challengeCorner.prompt: A store has adjusted cost \$5 per item, original SP \$8. They apply a 30% markdown. What is the profit or loss per item? (use word 'profit' or 'loss' with number, e.g., '0.60 profit')

hints: It’s the cost after accounting for spoilage.
questions.prompt: To avoid a loss, the sale price after markdown must be at least ___.
Adjusted cost \$12, original SP \$20. What is the maximum markdown percent (whole number) that still covers cost?
If adjusted cost is \$8 and the store must markdown to \$7 to sell quickly, what is the loss per unit? (number only, no $)

discoveryHook.scenario: A grocer has 50 cartons of strawberries that cost \$200. After two days, 10 cartons spoil. The remaining 40 are still fresh, but to sell them quickly, the grocer applies a 20% markdown off the original selling price of \$6 per carton. The sale price must still cover the adjusted cost.

examples.prompt: Adjusted cost per melon is \$4.00. The store priced them originally at \$6.00. Can the store take a 25% markdown and still cover cost?
examples.title: A – Can we markdown?
B – Loss decision
steps: Selling at \$4.80 loses \$0.20 per unit, but throwing away loses the entire \$5.00.
It is better to sell at a loss than to get nothing.
Sometimes recovering part of the cost is the best option.
examples.prompt: If the adjusted cost is \$5.00 and the best markdown price the market will accept is \$4.80, should the store sell or throw away? Explain.
examples.peerPrompt: Consider whether it's better to get some money back or nothing.

examples.title: C – Find markdown limit
examples.prompt: A cheese wheel costs the store \$18 (adjusted) and is originally priced at \$30. What is the maximum markdown percent they can offer without selling below cost?
steps: Original SP = 30, let p = markdown percent (decimal). Then 30 (1 – p) ≥ 18 → 1 – p ≥ 18/30 = 0.6 → p ≤ 0.4.

notes: Original SP should first be set to cover adjusted cost plus desired markup.
If the markdown price falls below adjusted cost, the item is sold at a loss.
formulaCard.title: Key Checks for Markdown on Perishables

explanation: After spoilage occurs, the effective cost of the remaining good units rises.
If a markdown is then applied to clear the remaining stock, the sale price must be ≥ adjusted cost to avoid a loss.
The original selling price is often set using a markup on the adjusted cost.
Then a markdown from that price can be taken, as long as the reduced price still exceeds the adjusted cost.
This approach is common for goods nearing their expiration date.

visuals.title: Perishable Markdown Scenario
visuals.caption: Even after a markdown, the sale price covers the adjusted cost and leaves a small profit.

blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid for Markdown and Perishable Problems

challengeCorner.prompt: A fish market buys 200 lbs of fish for \$800, spoilage 25%, markup 50% on adjusted cost, then 30% markdown. Find the final sale price per lb and profit per lb.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't forget to apply the markdown to the original selling price, not to the adjusted cost. [[imp:Markdown is a percent off the price tag, not off the cost.]]

teacherCues: Use the blueprint: Understand → Solve → Conclude, adapted for markdown/perishable scenarios.

explanation: Apply the blueprint systematically:
1. Understand: list total cost, total units, spoilage rate, desired markup percent, markdown percent.
2. Solve: compute expected good units, adjusted cost, original selling price (via markup), then sale price after markdown.
3. Conclude: compare sale price to adjusted cost to determine profit or loss.
This multi‑step approach prevents errors in complex real‑world problems.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Good Units} = \text{Total Units} \times (1 - \text{Spoilage Rate})$$ $$\text{Adjusted Cost} = \frac{\text{Total Cost}}{\text{Good Units}}$$ $$\text{Original SP} = \text{Adjusted Cost} \times (1 + \text{Markup \% on Cost})$$ $$\text{Sale Price} = \text{Original SP} \times (1 - \text{Markdown \%})$$
notes: Check that Sale Price ≥ Adjusted Cost.
If not, decide whether to sell at a loss or discard.
